title: Precompute the normals and clear the render state per touched cell
body: **What changes.** Four changes inside `BadPatchFinder::FindBadPatchesGeneral` and its two callers, and nothing outside them. A dead sixteen megabyte array is switched off, the render state is cleared per touched cell instead of over the whole grid, the normals are precomputed once instead of per appearance, and the two hot loops run in parallel. The c stage, untouched against changed, on the quiet bench. One pair of bars per seed on a logarithmic axis, with the factor over each pair. **Why.** This stage is the slowest thing anyone iterating on the patch generator waits for. None of the four changes alters a decision the stage makes. They remove work that was never read, work that was repeated, and work that was serial for no reason. **That the output does not move.** The whole downstream, all five stages, was run on fresh copies of two growth trees, once with the change and once without it, and every file either arm wrote was compared: 94,962 files, 0 differing. Each arm had its own copy, so no file is equal by being the same file. The two arms print one line differently, out of ten stage logs, and that line reports that nothing was skipped. **What it is worth.** One row per growth tree. The stage's own wall clock, four threads, one run at a time, each on a fresh copy, with the machine under a sixth of a core busy of 24 before each run: | growth tree | without the four changes | with them | factor | files compared, differing | |---|---|---|---:|---| | seed26, PHerc. 1447, 9,512 patches | 1,548.2 s, 1,574.0, 1,675.7 | 49.4 s, 51.8 | 31.11x | 48,888, 0 | | repeat, PHerc. 0139 | not timed | not timed | none | 46,074, 0 | The factor is the median of one arm over the median of the other, on the one tree that was timed. There is no average across trees, and the second tree carries the identity only. Why the large trees were not timed is said below. **How to check it yourself.** Build this branch and `main` at `62cbc21`, run the `c` stage on the same fresh copy of a growth tree with four threads, and time both. Then run the four stages after it on both arms and compare the two output trees file by file. They should be equal. --- `BadPatchFinder::FindBadPatchesGeneral` is the slowest stage for anyone iterating on the patch generator. Four changes inside it and its two callers, none of which changes a decision the stage makes: 1. **A dead array is switched off.** `distances[2000][2000]` is never read: `CollectDistanceStats` has no caller and its body computes nothing. Sixteen megabytes and the work of filling them. 2. **The render state is cleared per touched cell.** `ClearRendered` zeroed the whole grid for every pair and every chain. A patch touches a few thousand cells of a million, so the cells it touched are recorded and only those are cleared. 3. **The normals are precomputed.** They do not depend on the transform, so they are the same every time a patch reappears in a chain, and they were being recomputed each time. 4. **The two hot loops are parallel.** The loops over pairs and over chains are independent per element. The render state moved out of the class into a per element structure; the parallel loop computes **only the numbers**, into a vector indexed by element, and the printed lines, `badPatchScores`, `pairStats` and the reported chains are derived from those in a later serial pass, in the original order. That is why the output does not move. **One note for a reviewer.** `std::map::operator[]` inserts when the key is absent, so `(*patches)[p]` and `am[p]` inside a parallel loop would be a silent race on the map. In the parallel sections they are `at()`. ## What it is worth, measured on 22 September and not before The stage's own wall clock on one growth tree of PHerc. 1447, 9,512 patches and 21,436 relation rows, four threads, one run at a time, each on a fresh copy of the tree, with the machine between 0.05 and 0.12 cores busy of 24 before each run: | arm | runs | seconds | |---|---:|---| | without these four changes | 3 | 1,548.2, 1,574.0, 1,675.7 | | with them | 2 | 49.4, 51.8 | **31.11 times**, median over median, and 31.34 taking the smallest run of each arm. The spread within each arm is 8.24 per cent of its smallest on the slow side and 4.86 on the fast one, so the two ways of reading it agree to well inside the noise. Two things are said plainly rather than left out. **This is one tree**, a ribbon: the same measurement on the two large trees was not made, because at this factor it came to more than sixty hours each for a number this table already gives. And **one of the five runs had a disturbance inside it**, 24 seconds of one core from a watcher of another job of ours, on a run in the denominator; dropping it moves the factor to 30.14, which is inside the spread either way, and the table keeps every run that finished. ## What is not claimed **This change alone preserves the output, and the measurement is this change's own.** We ran the whole downstream, all five stages, on fresh copies of two growth trees, once with the change and once without it, and compared every file either arm wrote: **94,962 files, none differing**. One tree is a PHerc1447 growth (48,888 files), the other a PHerc0139 growth (46,074). Each arm had its own copy of the tree, so no file is equal by being the same file. The two arms do not print quite the same thing, and the difference is one line. On both trees, the arm with the change prints points skipped as off-grid: 0 and the arm without it does not print it at all. That is the whole of it: ten stage logs compared, two differing, one line each, and the line reports that nothing was skipped. An earlier text of ours reported byte equality of three output files on a frozen 218 patch reference case. That apparatus and its files are gone and we do not repeat its numbers; the table above stands on the run described here and not on that one. Nothing is claimed about memory either. The earlier text reported 72 MB becoming about 430 with sixteen threads; it has the same problem and is not repeated here. ## How it sits with the other pull request This branch is `main` plus this one patch. The other, `badpatchfinder-linear-enumeration`, is this branch plus three more changes to the same function, and it **cannot be cut from `main` without this one**: its patches fail to apply there and one hunk genuinely conflicts. Take them in either order as reviews, but they merge in this one.
